title: OpenCode 2.0
author: gmays
relevanceReason: 命中 4 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: OpenCode 2.0 is a major overhaul. It draws on millions of daily users' experience to deliver a system that can flex to everything an agent needs to be. There are quite a lot of new features, performance improvements, and bug fixes but here are some of the more impactful user-facing changes.The ServiceFrom the beginning OpenCode adopted a client/server model. However, this was not something it took advantage of by default and was mostly used by power users.In 2.0 this server now automatically runs as a single background process on your machine. When you open up a TUI, the web interface or the desktop app they're all talking to the same central process.opencodepid 48213RunningSessionsFix flaky testAdd dark modeReview changesIf you're using the programmatic client @opencode/client to make your own scripts, they will autodiscover the local service and just work. This is particularly useful for scheduled tasks. You can also call it via CLI by using opencode api commands.You can expose it to other hosts and run /pair or opencode pair to connect it to other applications. We have native apps in the works that take advantage of this flow.The APIThe old API grew haphazardly as we and the world collectively learned what agents are and should be. It was bad.We started from scratch and examined all the weird use cases across the millions of users who use OpenCode every day. It now supports nearly anything you need to be able to do.OpenCode is also aware of its own API and will call it to do useful things like moving the current session into a git worktree when starting new work.SessionNew sessionOpenCode~/appFix flaky upload testinterruptedMigrate config loadertab closedNew sessionthis session~/worktrees/rate-limitWe've also shipped a new client package @opencode/client that contains clients for vanilla JavaScript as well as Effect.review.tsimport { OpenCode } from "@opencode/client" import { Service } from "@opencode/client/service"
const endpoint = await Service.ensure() const client = OpenCode.make({ baseUrl: endpoint.url, headers: Service.headers(endpoint), })
const session = await client.session.create({ location: { directory: process.cwd() }, })

await client.session.prompt({ sessionID: session.id, text: "Review the current changes", })Code ModeThe models love to write code and OpenCode 2.0 takes advantage of that more than any other coding agent. We've built a minimal JavaScript interpreter in the @opencode/codemode package.SessionCode ModeMCP serversgithublinearsentryThis package ingests MCP servers or OpenAPI endpoints, converting them into functions that the agent can call in a script. It can run these scripts natively without the complexity of Node.js VMs or embedding complicated solutions like QuickJS.This lets your agent write scripts that can do things like call a tool, map over the results and call another tool. Single round trip instead of calling them one at a time.All MCP servers in 2.0 are opted into codemode by default. This means you can add a thousand of them with minimal context bloat and your agent will discover and compose them to get things done.Background TasksThe latest batch of models are incredibly good at orchestration and it is important for harnesses to let them express the full extent of that capability.SessionBackgroundFirst, we've added background subagents. This allows the primary agent to kick off some work to another one while it continues.This happens automatically but you can also trigger it manually - even with a different model. It lets you do things like “spawn a background fable subagent to review this code” while you keep prompting.Second, we've added background shell commands. The shell tool can be invoked asynchronously so long-running work does not have to block the primary agent. It'll be notified when things are complete.If any foreground shell command or subagent takes longer than you expect, you can hit a hotkey to move them to the background so you can keep prompting.PluginsAlthough OpenCode 1.0 had a plugin system, it never got the attention it needed. To correct that, we forced ourselves to implement nearly every OpenCode 2.0 feature as an internal plugin and there are now 80+ of them. This guarantees that the Plugin API stays well maintained.We've also promoted TUI plugins from experimental to stable. Since it is all powered by OpenTUI, you can build nearly anything. Here is an example of something useless.We also spent quite a lot of time ensuring everything in OpenCode 2.0 can be hot-reloaded. So it can write a plugin for itself mid-session and use it right away - we covered the design of this in a previous blogpost.You can ask OpenCode to build whatever plugin you want and it knows how to. But if you do want to read the docs, they are available here.The SDKOpenCode can also now be used as a library with the @opencode/sdk package. This is the exact same code that powers our CLI.This means you can strip it down and make your own flavor of OpenCode that runs on a server or in specialized environments like Durable Objects. And then you can connect to it from any OpenCode client since it speaks the standard OpenCode server protocol.It also has an optional Effect-based API.This one is still in development as things are shifting but you can already use it.UpgradingTo upgrade the CLI, make sure you're on the latest 1.x release, then run opencode upgrade --major.To upgrade your desktop app, download the latest here.There are some breaking changes.1.0 plugins will not work in 2.0Server API is completely differenttui.json config is moved to jsonThere are a lot of other changes but they are backwards compatible. It is worth pointing OpenCode at this doc so it can migrate things for you.

comments.author: ghrl
comments.textRawHtml:
I've been using OpenCode V2 since it first appeared on the website, and I can only repeat the positive views on usability, the client/server model and self-awareness/ability to edit it's config and write plugins.

I'd like to mention two other impressive things about OpenCode.

First, their issue tracker on GitHub works really well. They have the OpenCode GitHub App connected, and for any bug report it reads the issue, tests on the mentioned version and latest dev branch, and comments the findings along with a reproduction script. For TUI Bugs it even records a video. And all that in less than two minutes, usually.

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues?q=is%3Aissue+st...

Another thing they are working on is opentunnel, where you can tunnel services to https on <random>.opentunnel.xyz and its subdomains. What's notable is that the subdomain is persistent and unique to you, and a wildcard ssl cert is actually generated on your machine, so the platform cannot see the traffic. Their primary use case seems to be making the OpenCode Server usable from anywhere, but it can do much more with their cli:

https://opentunnel.xyz/

自从 OpenCode V2 首次出现在网站上以来，我一直在使用它，我只能重复对可用性、客户端/服务器模型和自我意识/编辑其配置和编写插件的能力的积极看法。

我想提一下关于 OpenCode 的另外两个令人印象深刻的事情。

首先，他们在 GitHub 上的问题跟踪器运行得非常好。他们连接了 OpenCode GitHub 应用程序，对于任何错误报告，它都会读取问题，对提到的版本和最新的开发分支进行测试，并对结果进行评论以及复制脚本。对于 TUI Bugs，它甚至会录制视频。通常，这一切都在不到两分钟的时间内完成。

https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues?q=is%3Aissue+st...

他们正在开发的另一件事是 opentunnel，您可以在其中将服务隧道传输到 .opentunnel.xyz 及其子域上的 https。值得注意的是，子域名对于您来说是持久且唯一的，并且通配符 ssl 证书实际上是在您的计算机上生成的，因此平台无法看到流量。他们的主要用例似乎是使 OpenCode Server 可以在任何地方使用，但它可以通过其 cli 执行更多操作：

https://opentunnel.xyz/

children.author: c-hendricks
children.textRawHtml:
> the client/server model

I see people talking about this being new in v2 everywhere but it's not the case. What's new is that it's the default (and also not really since `opencode service` and `opencode serve` start two different things). But in v1 it was very possible to run one opencode instance and have multiple clients connect to it (like Openchamber and neovim).
children.textZhHtml:
> 客户端/服务器模型

我看到人们到处都在谈论这是 v2 中的新功能，但事实并非如此。新鲜的是它是默认的（而且也不是真的，因为 `opencode service` 和 `opencode serve` 启动了两个不同的东西）。但在 v1 中，很可能运行一个 opencode 实例并让多个客户端连接到它（例如 Openchamber 和 neovim）。

comments.author: solarkraft
comments.textRawHtml:
It's good.

Many of the annoyances from V1 are gone. Skills and plugins reload automatically (finally). Tasks can be backgrounded (though I think this doesn't happen automatically yet). There's a built-in skill for editing the configuration (finally I can retire mine). The front-end got some love. Apparently they re-architected the loop around Effect. Sub-sessions can be communicated with better. Configuration is loaded from the folder the session is created in rather than where the server was started.

In general, this update largely takes OpenCode into the current age features-wise and is a good overhaul quality-wise. Just in time to stop my early switching away efforts, which would've been a pain because I know few other harnesses with such a strong server/client model.
comments.textZhHtml:
这很好。

V1 中的许多烦恼都消失了。技能和插件自动重新加载（最终）。任务可以在后台运行（尽管我认为这还不会自动发生）。有一个内置的编辑配置的技能（我终于可以退休了）。前端得到了一些爱。显然他们重新构建了 Effect 周围的循环。分会场可以更好的沟通。配置是从创建会话的文件夹加载的，而不是从服务器启动的位置加载的。

总的来说，此更新很大程度上将 OpenCode 纳入了当前时代的功能，并且在质量方面是一次很好的彻底改革。正好及时停止我早期的放弃努力，这将是一个痛苦，因为我知道很少有其他具有如此强大的服务器/客户端模型的工具。

children.author: everforward
children.textRawHtml:
Pi notably ships without MCP support (or it did, I can't remember if they're adding it to Pi main or just the durable one). From a vanilla Pi perspective, I'm pretty sure but not positive that it can't. It would have to install an MCP plugin, and you would have to re-launch Pi to load that plugin.

It does have native tools, but they're also in plugins that aren't hot-reloaded. The LLM would have to write the tool, you close Pi and re-open it before it was available.

> Would you consider that a gap in security posturing?

Honestly, I think trying to secure the harness is a lost cause for the same reasons SELinux never really took off. They solve a real problem in a way so painful people would rather just live dangerously.

I actually wrote a thing to implement my security posture https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss TLDR it pretends to be an ACP agent, but runs the agent inside Docker (with optional bind mounts) and proxies the ACP connection into the container.

I'm also tinkering with WASM-based plugins in the ACP proxy to add some additional security and compliance posturing at the protocol layer (ie agnostic to what the underlying agent is). E.g. I slapped together a plugin that will automatically cancel a prompt mid-turn if an OpenRouter API token shows up in a) the prompt, b) agent output/thinking, c) agent tool calls. ([1], [2], [3]). The grand vision is slapping centralized management on that so security and compliance teams get a "firewall" of sorts to prevent leaking secrets, filter bash commands, censor PII, yada, yada.

1. Screenshot of it blocking something in Zed https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/what-is-abyss/#i-am-not-... (I need to add buffering so it doesn't output any of the key)

2. Implementation of ^ https://github.com/SethCurry/abyss/blob/main/plugins/secrets...

3. Plugin architecture docs https://abyss.scurry.io/docs/guides/04-plugins/02-developing...

children.author: everforward
children.textRawHtml:
I looked and will give it a try, but haven’t had a chance yet because life.

I had debated building something like this, and I really want to see what the other fork in the path looks like.

One of the core tenants of mine is to not impose a workflow or set of tooling on the user. I specifically opted not to go with k8s because access to local files is going to be a pain, and I think people will still expect that. There’s all sorts of “I need this binary that’s not in APT”, or “you need this cert to test, and we can’t commit it” stumbling blocks.

Yours feels like it’s pushing me into an unfamiliar workflow, but opinionated tools are often better so it’s worth a try.

My only direct criticism is that I think k8s is a bad way to go for this (but is probably what people expect). For personal use, k8s is more than I want to deal with. For work use, I suspect lambdas would be cheaper and avoid a ton of maintenance junk. We tend to think of agents as a persistent process, but they’re sort of not. They’re a stateless process that is effectively dead until a new message comes in, let it be dead until something else comes down the pipe.
